TRAFFIC ENFORCEMENT AGENT: Most of what shows up as "paperwork" in this job is not paperwork. Writing a summons looks like a clerical task, but it is an appealable record affirmed by the agent who observed the violation — so it stays with a person no matter how good the software gets. Where AI genuinely helps is the surrounding load: drafting radio and dispatch messages, pulling plate and complaint records together before you decide, and preparing the training material a new agent needs. The parts that stay yours split two ways worth knowing apart — patrolling and spotting a missing sign stay yours because they need a person on the street, which technology may eventually change; issuing the summons stays yours because the law says a person issues it, which no model release will change. The leverage is that the more the routine lookups are handled for you, the more of your day is the observation and the judgment only you can sign for.
SCHOOL SAFETY AGENT: The clearest case first: apprehending or removing someone, and using force when it is necessary, cannot be handed to a system at all — that authority is vested in a person, and that is a rule question, not a capability question. Answering off-hours phone calls and taking messages is at the other end and is the kind of thing software can carry outright. In between sits the bulk of the job — authorizing who comes in and out, writing up the day's incidents, deciding when to call police or fire — where AI can draft and organize but a named person still has to stand behind the result. Be skeptical of anything that offers to write your incident reports for you: those reports are discoverable and they are read as your account of what happened, so a fast draft you did not really check is a risk transferred onto you. Patrolling, answering an alarm, and reading a room full of students stay with you because presence is the job.
EMERGENCY MEDICAL SPECIALIST-EMT: This is the job in this whole set that AI touches least, and the reason is not sentiment — it is that almost every task is a physical act on a person under a certification that belongs to you. Assessing a patient, administering care, comforting someone who is frightened, decontaminating the bus afterward: none of that is producible by a model, and the scope of practice is licensed to a human besides. Where AI can actually help is the handoff — structuring what you tell the receiving hospital or the dispatcher, and coordinating with fire and police on a scene — so that less of your attention goes to relaying and more goes to the patient. One honest caveat: driving the unit is on this list because a person drives it today, and that is the one item here that could change with technology rather than with law. Your certification and your hands are the leverage, and nothing on the horizon reaches them.
CARETAKER: The city calls this title Caretaker; the work is building cleaning and maintenance for public housing, and naming it accurately is the first step to saying anything true about it. Nearly all of it — restrooms, floors, trash, glass, mixing and handling cleaning chemicals safely — requires a person physically doing it, so it is among the least exposed work in this data, not the most. The office-shaped edges are the exposed part: ordering supplies against what actually gets used is the kind of thing software can simply run, and flagging a repair that needs a manager's attention is something AI can help you write up faster and more clearly. That inversion is worth carrying around, because the assumption usually runs the other way. It also means the thing that raises your value here is the part no system sees: you are the one who notices the failing system before it becomes an emergency, and the better your report, the sooner it gets fixed.
SERGEANT-: This is the clearest case in the whole tool of why a single job-level number would mislead you. Half of a sergeant's listed work AI can genuinely help with — briefing subordinates, summarizing amended law and new procedure, keeping departmental logs and reports moving. The other half stays with you for a reason that has nothing to do with how good the software gets: signing off on an investigation, making a misconduct finding against a member of your command, authorizing a promotion or transfer, directing the chain of custody over evidence. Those are acts the law vests in a person, and no model release touches them — which is different from the EMT down the hall, whose human-anchored work is human because it needs a body present, and could erode as technology improves. Same label on the page, opposite futures, and that is exactly what one score would erase.
TEACHER- PER SESSION: This is the largest title in New York City and it is not a job at all — it is how the Department of Education pays teachers hourly for after-school and summer work. The people under it are overwhelmingly the same people already counted under TEACHER, so any AI analysis of this line would double-count them and describe nobody accurately. The tell is right on this page: the median annual salary is null, because almost nobody is paid annually under it. If you hold this title, the honest answer is that your exposure question belongs to your actual teaching title, not this pay code. We would rather report 78,618 rows as a documented exclusion than invent a job to put a number on.
ELECTION WORKER: Poll work is a civic stipend role, not an occupation, and the city's own payroll structure says so — it keeps a separate agency for poll workers with 36,732 rows, apart from the 1,027 people who actually staff the Board of Elections year-round. There are zero salaried rows here. Coding this as a job would launder a stipend into an occupation and then generate an AI risk score for it, which would be meaningless for the tens of thousands of New Yorkers who do it once or twice a year. The useful question for this population is about the election process, not about anyone's career exposure. So we stop.
STUDENT AIDE: This is a hiring category rather than a job — students placed across many different city agencies doing many different things under one payroll label. There is no single set of tasks to analyze, so there is no honest task-level answer, and a job-level score would be an average across work that has nothing in common. If you are in this title, the question worth asking is what the specific placement involves, which the payroll file does not record. Naming that gap is more useful to you than a confident number would be.
JOB TRAINING PARTICIPANT: The title names the program someone is enrolled in, not the work they do — and the payroll data shows it: 18 salaried rows out of 4,021. There is no occupation here to describe, so there is nothing honest to say about AI exposure for it. That is a finding about how the city classifies people, not a gap in our data. For anyone in this title, the meaningful analysis attaches to the job the training leads to, and that is where this tool should point you next.
F/T SCHOOL AIDE: This one is different from the titles we skip, and the difference matters: these are 9,217 real workers doing real jobs. The problem is that the work sits in three completely different occupational families — education support, office and clerical, and food service — depending on the school assignment, and no single occupation code spans them. Picking one would misclassify most of the people under the title. Resolving it needs Department of Education school-assignment data, which is not in the payroll file. So the honest answer today is that we can tell you the title is real and we cannot yet tell you the tasks — and we would rather say that than guess.
COLLEGE ASSISTANT: Real work, and a real gap. This one title covers clerical, tutoring, laboratory, and library assignments across CUNY's community colleges — genuinely different occupations sharing one payroll label. Any single occupation code would describe a minority of the people in it, so a task-level analysis would be confidently wrong rather than usefully approximate. Worth noting that this population is much larger than people assume: CUNY's community colleges are city-funded and appear in this payroll file under their own campus names. Getting an answer here means splitting the title by assignment first, which is work we have not done rather than work we are hiding.
CITY SEASONAL AIDE: There is no honest AI answer for this title, and that is the finding rather than a gap. City Seasonal Aide is a hiring category, not a job — in FY2025 only 17 of its 2,414 payroll rows carry an annual salary, and the people under it are doing genuinely different work in different agencies. Any tool that hands you a single risk number for this title is quietly averaging a lifeguard, a parks crew member, and an office temp into one figure that is wrong for every one of them. What a person in this title actually needs first is the work described accurately — which tasks, in which agency — before anyone says a word about automation. So we stop here on purpose, and the eval that gates this demo fails the build if we ever fill it in with a guess.
